- CENTRAL CONTRIBUTION: This work introduces TsetFall, a comprehensive, fine-grained, and publicly available dataset meticulously generated for human fall detection research, addressing existing dataset limitations in size, diversity, representativeness, and real-world complexity by including precise object location annotations and diverse scenarios. The dataset's annotation process was notably expedited and enhanced by a novel AI-assisted technique devised by the authors, enabling detailed object-level annotations for training and evaluating advanced computer vision algorithms.

- PROBLEM AND CONTEXT: Human fall detection remains an underdeveloped area, particularly in utilizing dynamic images for analysis. Existing fall detection datasets commonly suffer from significant limitations, including small video collections, restricted ranges of actions, limited camera perspectives, and unvaried lighting conditions. Critically, these datasets often lack the complexity of real-world scenarios, frequently omitting distracting objects and offering only one or two camera angles, alongside a dearth of fine-grained annotations, such as bounding geometries of objects of interest. This scarcity of crucial information detrimentally impacts the performance and accuracy of fall detection systems. The urgent need for comprehensive datasets is underscored by the global population aging, with the United Nations anticipating a near doubling of the population aged 65 and older to 1.5 billion by 2050, and falls being the second leading cause of accidental injury deaths worldwide, accounting for an estimated 684,000 fatal falls annually.

- METHOD/SYSTEM: The TsetFall dataset comprises 144 videos, featuring high-resolution RGB and infrared images (1920x1080 pixels) captured from four analogue Intelbras VHD 3220DG cameras with night vision, positioned in the four corners of a standard indoor room (3.2m x 2.8m x 2.8m) at a height of 2.8m (Fig. 2). The cameras were connected to an Intelbras Mhdx 1104 DVR via coaxial cable. The data acquisition involved a healthy 31-year-old male Computer Science postgraduate from Universidade de Fortaleza, enacting 36 diverse activities (Fig. 3) including various fall types (forward, backward, lateral, others, with an inflatable mattress for safety) and Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) such as walking, sitting, standing, and exercising. The scenes incorporate distractor objects and variable lighting conditions, including "in the dark" sequences, to simulate real-world complexity (Fig. 1). Video recording was managed via Python-implemented software utilizing Real-Time Streaming Protocol (RTSP) and the OpenCV library, saving footage in AVI format using the XVID codec.

The dataset's fine-grained annotation process combined human supervision with an AI-assisted technique. Initial human annotations provided Axis-Aligned Bounding Boxes (AABBs) for the individual's location at four-frame intervals for each of the four distinct camera viewpoints, along with class labels. The defined class set for fall detection includes Confounding (C) for fall-precursor movements, Fallen (FN), Falling (FG), and Not Fallen (NF). This initial human annotation served as "reference frames." The AI-assisted technique then propagated these annotations to unannotated frames using a two-step approach: first, by leveraging temporal coherence, and second, by combining an Object Tracking algorithm [10] and an Object Detection algorithm [11], [12]. The object tracker (pre-trained on COCO, TrackingNet, LaSOT, and GOT10k datasets) propagated the approximate person location, while a pre-trained Object Detector (COCO dataset) refined the bounding boxes. To select the best detection, the Jaccard Similarity Calculation (Intersection Over Union, IoU) (Eq. 1: J(A, B) = |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|) was used, selecting the detection with the highest IoU between the tracker output and candidate detector outputs (Fig. 4). This process yielded 56,591 total annotated frames across all cameras and sequences, with detailed class distributions (Table I).

For baseline evaluation, four pre-trained YOLOv8 architectures (YOLOv8l, YOLOv8m, YOLOv8s, YOLOv8n) [18] from the COCO dataset were employed. These models were trained for 200 epochs, with an early stopping tolerance of 50 epochs for mAP improvement, using Stochastic Gradient Descent [19] as the optimizer with an initial learning rate of 0.01. The dataset for training utilized bounding box annotations from cameras 1, 2, and 3, reserving camera 4 for validation. For simplified evaluation, the classes were mapped: FN and FG to "Fall," and NF and C to "NoFall." A frame was classified as "Fall" if at least one detected object belonged to the "Fall" class, and "NoFall" otherwise or if no objects were detected.

- RESULTS AND METRICS:
The baseline YOLOv8 models demonstrated robust performance. On the human-annotated TsetFall subset (Camera 4), YOLOv8n achieved the highest mAP IOU [0.5:0.95] at 65.61%, mAP IOU 0.5 at 89.97%, mAP IOU 0.75 at 74.39%, and AR [20] IOU [0.5:0.95] maxDets 10 at 72.87% (Table III). On the complete AI-assisted annotated set (Camera 4), YOLOv8l achieved the highest mAP IOU [0.5:0.95] at 68.17%, mAP IOU 0.5 at 85.59%, mAP IOU 0.75 at 81.27%, and AR [20] IOU [0.5:0.95] maxDets 10 at 74.29% (Table IV). For fall detection specific metrics using the simplified Fall/NoFall classes, YOLOv8l achieved a Sensitivity of 98.96%, Specificity of 99.94%, and a Geometric Mean of 99.45% (where Geometric Mean = √[Sensitivity × Specificity]). YOLOv8s also showed strong performance with Sensitivity 98.64%, Specificity 99.78%, and Geometric Mean 99.21% (Table V). A comparison with existing RGB datasets (Table VI) highlights TsetFall's advantages: 144 videos, 4 multi-camera viewpoints (4 corners), 1920x1080 resolution, RGB and infrared data, 8 falls per viewpoint (32 total), 28 ADLs per viewpoint (112 total), and comprehensive AI-assisted and human-supervised object-level annotations including subject locations, which none of the other datasets (Multicam Fall [21], UR Fall Detection [22], UMA Fall [23]) provide comprehensively.

- LIMITATIONS: The TsetFall dataset primarily features single actor scenes and is confined to indoor environments at a single location. While comprehensive for its scope, these aspects limit its direct applicability for multi-person fall detection or scenarios in diverse outdoor settings.

- KEY CONCEPTS: Human Fall Detection, TsetFall Dataset, Fine-grained Annotation, AI-assisted Annotation, Object Detection, YOLOv8, Object Tracking, Axis-Aligned Bounding Boxes (AABBs), Jaccard Similarity (Intersection Over Union - IoU), Activities of Daily Living (ADLs), RGB and Infrared Imagery, Camera Perspectives, Stochastic Gradient Descent, Mean Average Precision (mAP), Sensitivity, Specificity, Geometric Mean.
